--- title: "Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared" description: "Where tornadoes happen: the United States state by state since 1950, how Canada's count compares, when they strike, how strong and how deadly they are, the worst events, and whether there are more of them." author: "" date: "27 November 2026" --- ## What is this? A tornado is a narrow, violently rotating column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. People think of the American Plains, and the United States does report more tornadoes than any other country we can count. But there is no single open database of the world's tornadoes, so this story does what the data allow: it counts the United States closely, sets Canada beside it, and says plainly what cannot be compared. It asks five questions: 1. **Where do tornadoes happen?** 2. **When do they strike?** 3. **How strong and how deadly are they?** 4. **Which were the worst?** 5. **Are there more of them than there used to be?** This is one of a series on natural disasters: see the [overview](ILLUSTRATION_NATURAL_DISASTERS.html) and [Floods](ILLUSTRATION_WORLD_FLOODS.html). The data come from two places, downloaded when the page is rendered: - **The United States**: the tornado database of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's **Storm Prediction Center** (SPC), one row for each tornado since 1950, with its date and time, the state, the start and end points, the length and width of its path, the rating, and the people injured and killed ([SPC severe weather database](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/#data)). It is made of the reports that the National Weather Service's offices send in ([format description](https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/SPC_severe_database_description.pdf)). The file used here is the one with single tracks: a tornado that crosses a state line is one row, in the state where it touched down. - **Canada**: the event summaries of the **Northern Tornadoes Project**, founded at Western University in 2017, which investigates tornadoes by ground, drone, aerial and satellite surveys ([Northern Tornadoes Project](https://www.uwo.ca/ntp/)). **The rating of a tornado** is not a measurement of its wind. Since February 2007 the National Weather Service rates a tornado on the **Enhanced Fujita scale**, from EF0 to EF5, from the damage that it leaves: an EF0 is estimated at 65 to 85 miles per hour (the gust of three seconds), an EF1 at 86 to 110, an EF2 at 111 to 135, an EF3 at 136 to 165, an EF4 at 166 to 200 and an EF5 at more than 200 ([National Weather Service](https://www.weather.gov/oun/efscale)). Before 2007 the original **Fujita scale** (F0 to F5) was used, in the same way. This page writes EF0 to EF5 for both. A tornado is rated by what it destroys, so one that crosses empty land can get a low rating whatever its wind. **Europe is missing, on purpose.** The European Severe Weather Database, kept by the European Severe Storms Laboratory, lets a guest browse only recent events; the full data need a request for restricted access ([ESWD](https://eswd.eu/)). A study of its reports from 1950 to 2015 finds that tornadoes do occur in Europe, with injuries, deaths and damage, "although their reported frequencies and intensities are lower compared with the United States" ([Antonescu et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1175/bams-d-16-0171.1)). That is all this page can say about Europe from what it has read. --- ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("plotly", "jsonlite")) library(plotly) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the SPC file of single tornado tracks since 1950, named after the last year it holds: try the # latest years first this_year<-as.integer(format(Sys.Date(),"%Y")) tor<-NULL for(y in this_year:2020) { tor<-tryCatch(read.csv(paste0("https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-",y, "_actual_tornadoes.csv")), error=function(e) NULL) if(!is.null(tor)) break } # the Northern Tornadoes Project's event summaries (Canada), a thousand rows at a time ntp_url<-paste0("https://services.arcgis.com/rGKxabTU9mcXMw7k/arcgis/rest/services/", "NTP_Event_Summaries_stakeholder/FeatureServer/0/query") ntp<-do.call(rbind,lapply(seq(0,9000,by=1000),function(offset) { r<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(ntp_url,"?where=1%3D1&outFields=Year,event_type,province", "&returnGeometry=false&resultOffset=",offset, "&resultRecordCount=1000&f=json")) if(length(r$features)==0) NULL else r$features$attributes })) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} first_year<-min(tor$yr) last_year<-max(tor$yr) first_ten<-first_year:(first_year+9) last_ten<-(last_year-9):last_year # the rating: -9 means that the tornado has no rating ratings<-c("EF0","EF1","EF2","EF3","EF4","EF5") tor$rating<-factor(ifelse(tor$mag<0,"Unrated",ratings[pmax(tor$mag,0)+1]), levels=c("Unrated",ratings)) n_unrated<-sum(tor$mag<0) state_name<-function(s) { result<-ifelse(s%in%state.abb,state.name[match(s,state.abb)],s) return(result) } # the states: 50 states, with their area (the R datasets) and the census division they are in areas<-data.frame(st=state.abb, state=state.name, km2=state.area*2.589988, division=as.character(state.division)) tor_states<-tor[tor$st%in%areas$st,] # the time of day: the SPC puts all times, but a few, on central standard time (3 in the column tz); # the sun's time at the place is the clock in Greenwich (central standard time plus six hours) plus # one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude hms<-do.call(rbind,strsplit(tor$time,":")) tor$clock<-as.numeric(hms[,1])+as.numeric(hms[,2])/60 tor$sun_hour<-floor((tor$clock+6+tor$slon/15)%%24) timed<-tor[tor$tz==3&tor$slon!=0,] n_other_clock<-sum(tor$tz!=3) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} red<-"#d62728" gray<-"#bdbdbd" dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes blue<-"#2171b5" # one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the maps and the calendar blues<-c("#eff3ff","#c6dbef","#9ecae1","#6baed6","#4292c6","#2171b5","#084594") # one hue for the ratings, from EF0 to EF5; the unrated are grey rating_colors<-c(Unrated="#d9d9d9",EF0="#c6dbef",EF1="#9ecae1",EF2="#6baed6",EF3="#4292c6", EF4="#2171b5",EF5="#084594") # the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(), margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) { note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left", yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray)) result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"), yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),margin=margin, annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>% config(displaylogo=FALSE) return(result) } legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom") # a colour scale of steps for classes numbered 1, 2, ... (with zmin = 0.5): one colour for each # class color_steps<-function(colors) { n<-length(colors) result<-do.call(c, lapply(seq_len(n),function(i) list(list((i-1)/n,colors[i]),list(i/n,colors[i])))) return(result) } # numbers in the text number<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE) return(result) } percent<-function(x,digits=0) { result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%") return(result) } one<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE) return(result) } two<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE) return(result) } # a change in per cent, with its sign change_text<-function(x) { result<-paste0(ifelse(x>=0,"+","−"),round(abs(x)),"%") return(result) } and_list<-function(x) { if(length(x)<2) { return(paste(x)) } result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1)) return(result) } # a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one # without a trend chance<-function(x,years) { p<-cor.test(years,x,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value result<-if(p<0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100*p)) return(result) } # a date as "27 April 2011" long_date<-function(x) { result<-trimws(format(as.Date(x),"%e %B %Y")) return(result) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the unrated tornadoes in the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale, and the tornadoes that the SPC # rated afterwards from the damage (fc = 1, from 1953 to 1982) n_all<-nrow(tor) unrated_years<-aggregate(cbind(share=mag<0)~yr,data=tor[tor$yr>=2007,],FUN=mean) unrated_years$share<-100*unrated_years$share first_unrated<-min(tor$yr[tor$mag<0&tor$yr>=2007]) rated_early<-tor[tor$fc==1,] ``` ::: **Some tornadoes have no rating.** 1,546 of the 73,458 tornadoes (2.1%) are coded -9, "unknown". For 1953 to 1982 the SPC has filled in an estimated rating, from the property loss and the length of the path, for 1,863 tornadoes that had none; the file marks them. The 1,546 that remain unrated come from 2007 on, and from 2019 on they are 10% to 20% of the tornadoes of a year. The documentation does not say why. This page counts them in the totals, shows them apart in the tables, and, where a trend depends on the ratings, tests what happens if all of them were strong (section 5). **Times are those of the sun.** The SPC converts the time of a tornado to central standard time, whatever the state (37 tornadoes are on another clock). A tornado in Georgia at 17:00 central standard time struck at six in the evening by the clock there. To compare places, section 2 turns each time into **the sun's time at the place where the tornado began**, from its longitude: an hour for every 15 degrees. --- ## 1. Where do tornadoes happen? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} last_eight<-(last_year-7):last_year us_a_year<-sum(tor$yr%in%last_eight)/length(last_eight) ntp$Year<-as.integer(ntp$Year) canada_tornadoes<-ntp[ntp$event_type%in%c("tornado_over_land","tornado_over_water")& ntp$Year%in%last_eight,] canada_a_year<-nrow(canada_tornadoes)/length(last_eight) canada_water<-100*mean(canada_tornadoes$event_type=="tornado_over_water") # the states since 2006, the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale: the tornadoes, those of EF2 and # above and those of EF3 and above since<-2006 years_since<-last_year-since+1 by_state<-aggregate(cbind(all=1,ef2=mag>=2,ef3=mag>=3)~st,data=tor_states[tor_states$yr>=since,], FUN=sum) by_state<-merge(by_state,areas,by="st",all.x=TRUE) by_state$per_10k<-by_state$all/years_since/by_state$km2*1e4 by_state$ef2_per_10k<-by_state$ef2/years_since/by_state$km2*1e4 by_state$a_year<-by_state$all/years_since by_count<-by_state[order(-by_state$all),] by_density<-by_state[order(-by_state$per_10k),] by_strong<-by_state[order(-by_state$ef2_per_10k),] top_density<-by_density$state[1:3] # the state with the most tornadoes, and its density texas<-by_state[by_state$st=="TX",] rank_texas_density<-which(by_density$st=="TX") n_states<-nrow(by_state) ``` ::: **The United States reports about 1,346 tornadoes a year; Canada's project finds about 112, and for Europe there is no open count.** From 2018 to 2025 the United States had 1,346 a year on average and Canada 112 (15% of them over water, which the Canadian figures count). The two numbers are **not** a fair comparison. They come from different ways of finding tornadoes, and a tornado that nobody reports or surveys is not counted anywhere. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(place=c("United States","Canada","Europe"), a_year=c(number(us_a_year),number(canada_a_year),"no open count"), source=c(paste0("SPC database: reports sent in by National Weather ", "Service offices"), paste0("Northern Tornadoes Project: surveys on the ground, ", "by drone, from the air and from satellites"), paste0("European Severe Weather Database: browsing is limited to ", "recent events; the study of Antonescu et al. ", "finds fewer reports than in the United States"))), col.names=c("",paste0("Tornadoes a year, ",min(last_eight),"–",max(last_eight)), "Where it comes from"),align="lrl") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | Tornadoes a year, 2018–2025|Where it comes from | |:-------------|---------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| |United States | 1,346|SPC database: reports sent in by National Weather Service offices | |Canada | 112|Northern Tornadoes Project: surveys on the ground, by drone, from the air and from satellites | |Europe | no open count|European Severe Weather Database: browsing is limited to recent events; the study of Antonescu et al. finds fewer reports than in the United States | ::: ::: **In the United States, Texas has the most tornadoes, but the most for their size are in Mississippi.** Texas had the most tornadoes from 2006 to 2025, 119 a year, but it is large. Per area, Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois come first, with 5.40, 4.92 and 4.51 tornadoes a year for every 10,000 square kilometres; Texas is only 24th of the 50 states, with 1.72. For the strong tornadoes (EF2 and above) the order is Mississippi, Alabama and Kentucky: 0.90, 0.81 and 0.54. Hover over a state to see its numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classes<-c(0,0.1,0.5,1,2,3,4,Inf) class_names<-c("Under 0.1","0.1–0.5","0.5–1","1–2","2–3","3–4","4 or more") by_state$class<-as.integer(cut(by_state$per_10k,classes,right=FALSE)) plot_ly(by_state,type="choropleth",locationmode="USA-states",locations=~st,z=~class,zmin=0.5, zmax=7.5,colorscale=color_steps(blues),marker=list(line=list(color="white",width=0.6)), text=~paste0(state,": ",two(per_10k)," a year per 10,000 km²
",one(a_year), " tornadoes a year, ",one(ef2/years_since)," of them EF2 or above"), hoverinfo="text", colorbar=list(title=list(text="Tornadoes
a year per
10,000 km²"),tickvals=1:7, ticktext=class_names,len=0.8,thickness=14)) %>% chart(paste0("Tornadoes a year per 10,000 km², ",since,"–",last_year), "NOAA Storm Prediction Center; areas: R datasets (state.area). 50 states.", geo=list(scope="usa",projection=list(type="albers usa"),showlakes=FALSE), margin=list(t=50,b=40,l=0,r=0),note_y=-0.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The strongest tornadoes show where the damage is. The map shows where the most violent ones began, every EF3, EF4 and EF5 tornado from 1950 to 2025: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} strong<-tor[tor$mag>=3&tor$slon!=0&tor$slat!=0,] strong_dots<-function(p,x,color,name) { result<-add_trace(p,data=x,type="scattergeo",mode="markers",lon=~round(slon,2),lat=~round(slat,2), name=name,marker=list(color=color,size=4,opacity=0.55),hoverinfo="skip") return(result) } plot_ly() %>% strong_dots(strong[strong$mag==3,],blue,"EF3") %>% strong_dots(strong[strong$mag>=4,],red,"EF4 and EF5") %>% chart(paste0("Where EF3 or stronger tornadoes began, ",first_year,"–",last_year), "NOAA Storm Prediction Center. A dot is the start of a tornado.", geo=list(scope="usa",projection=list(type="albers usa"),showlakes=FALSE), legend=c(legend_top,list(y=1.0)),margin=list(t=70,b=40,l=0,r=0),note_y=-0.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} violent<-tor_states[tor_states$mag>=4,] division_of<-function(s) { result<-areas$division[match(s,areas$st)] return(result) } violent_by_division<-sort(table(division_of(violent$st)),decreasing=TRUE) violent_share<-100*violent_by_division/sum(violent_by_division) divisions_names<-function(d) { result<-and_list(areas$state[areas$division==d]) return(result) } ``` ::: Most of the violent ones, the EF4 and EF5, began in two census divisions: the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) had 32% of them and the West South Central division (Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas) 24%. --- ## 2. When do they strike? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} month_share<-function(x) { result<-100*tabulate(x$mo,12)/nrow(x) return(result) } all_months<-month_share(tor) strong_months<-month_share(tor[tor$mag>=3,]) peak_month<-which.max(all_months) three_months<-function(s) { result<-sapply(1:12,function(m) sum(s[(m-1+0:2)%%12+1])) return(result) } best_three<-which.max(three_months(all_months)) best_three_share<-max(three_months(all_months)) winter_share<-sum(all_months[c(12,1,2)]) strong_winter<-sum(strong_months[c(12,1,2)]) hour_share<-100*tabulate(timed$sun_hour+1,24)/nrow(timed) peak_hour<-which.max(hour_share)-1 afternoon<-sum(hour_share[(15:19)+1]) # 15:00 to 19:59 night<-timed$sun_hour<=5 night_tornadoes<-100*mean(night) night_deaths<-100*sum(timed$fat[night])/sum(timed$fat) night_strong<-100*mean(night[timed$mag>=3]) # the share of the EF3 and above that began at night hour_label<-function(h) { result<-paste0(sprintf("%02d",h),":00") return(result) } ``` ::: **May is the peak month, and each part of the country peaks at its own time.** 22% of all tornadoes since 1950 began in May, and 54% in the three months of April to June. The strong ones (EF3 and above) are more spread out over the year than the weak ones: 11% of them came in December, January and February, against 8% of all tornadoes. The calendar shows, for each census division, the share of its tornadoes that came in each month. The divisions are ordered from the one with the most tornadoes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the tornadoes of each division in each month, and their share of the division's tornadoes division_months<-data.frame(division=division_of(tor_states$st),mo=tor_states$mo) by_division<-aggregate(cbind(n=mo)~division+mo,data=division_months,FUN=length) by_division$share<-100*by_division$n/ave(by_division$n,by_division$division,FUN=sum) by_division<-by_division[order(by_division$division,by_division$mo),] # the divisions, from the one with the most tornadoes counts<-table(division_months$division) division_order<-names(counts)[order(-counts)] by_division$class<-as.integer(cut(by_division$share,c(-Inf,2,5,10,15,20,Inf))) division_classes<-c("Under 2%","2–5%","5–10%","10–15%","15–20%","20% or more") plot_ly(by_division,x=~mo,y=~division,z=~class,type="heatmap",zmin=0.5,zmax=6.5, colorscale=color_steps(blues[2:7]),xgap=2,ygap=2, text=~paste0(division,", ",month.abb[mo],": ",one(share),"% of its tornadoes"), hoverinfo="text", colorbar=list(title=list(text="Share of a division's tornadoes in the month",side="top"), orientation="h",x=0,xanchor="left",y=-0.1,yanchor="top",tickvals=1:6, ticktext=division_classes,len=0.9,thickness=12,tickfont=list(size=10))) %>% chart("When each part of the country has its tornadoes", paste0("NOAA Storm Prediction Center, ",first_year,"–",last_year, ". Census divisions of the 50 states."), x_axis=list(tickvals=1:12,ticktext=month.abb,showgrid=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE), y_axis=list(categoryorder="array",categoryarray=rev(division_order),showgrid=FALSE), margin=list(l=150,t=60,b=120,r=10),note_y=-0.36) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the busiest month of each division (the first one, if two are equal) division_peak<-do.call(rbind, lapply(split(by_division,by_division$division), function(x) x[which.max(x$share),])) peak_of<-function(d) { result<-month.name[division_peak$mo[division_peak$division==d]] return(result) } peak_share_of<-function(d) { result<-percent(division_peak$share[division_peak$division==d]) return(result) } south_east<-"East South Central" plains<-"West North Central" ``` ::: In the East South Central division (Alabama, Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee) the busiest month is April (22% of its tornadoes); in the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) it is June (27%). The chart shows the seasons of each division; it does not say why they differ. **Late afternoon and evening.** By the sun's time at the place where they began, the busiest hour of the day is 16:00 to 17:00, and 52% of all tornadoes began between 15:00 and 20:00. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hours<-data.frame(hour=0:23,share=hour_share) plot_ly(hours,x=~hour,y=~share,type="bar",marker=list(color=ifelse(hours$hour==peak_hour,red,gray)), customdata=~hour_label(hour), hovertemplate="%{customdata}: %{y:.1f}% of the tornadoes", showlegend=FALSE) %>% chart("What time of day tornadoes begin", paste0("NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Share of tornadoes that began in each hour, ", "by the sun's time, ",first_year,"–",last_year,". Red: the busiest hour."), x_axis=list(tickvals=seq(0,21,3),ticktext=hour_label(seq(0,21,3)),showgrid=FALSE), y_axis=list(ticksuffix="%",rangemode="tozero"),bargap=0.15,margin=list(t=60,b=70), note_y=-0.14) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Few begin at night, and they are somewhat deadlier.** Between midnight and 06:00 began 7% of the tornadoes, and 9% of the deaths were from them. Among the EF3 and stronger tornadoes, 8% began at night. --- ## 3. How strong and how deadly are they? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # each rating: the tornadoes, the deaths and the injured, and their shares by_rating<-aggregate(cbind(n=1,deaths=fat,injured=inj)~rating,data=tor,FUN=sum) by_rating$share<-100*by_rating$n/sum(by_rating$n) by_rating$death_share<-100*by_rating$deaths/sum(by_rating$deaths) by_rating$per_thousand<-1000*by_rating$deaths/by_rating$n of_rating<-function(r,column) { result<-by_rating[[column]][by_rating$rating==r] return(result) } rated_n<-sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating!="Unrated"]) weak_share<-100*sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating%in%c("EF0","EF1")])/rated_n violent_n<-sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating%in%c("EF4","EF5")]) violent_tor_share<-100*violent_n/sum(by_rating$n) violent_death_share<-sum(by_rating$death_share[by_rating$rating%in%c("EF4","EF5")]) total_deaths<-sum(tor$fat) total_injured<-sum(tor$inj) deaths_ef0<-of_rating("EF0","deaths") ``` ::: **Most tornadoes are weak; most of the deaths come from the strongest.** Of the tornadoes that have a rating, 81% were EF0 or EF1. The 656 EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of all of them, and 61% of the 6,341 people killed from 1950 to 2025 died in them. An EF5 killed on average 22 people, an EF0 one in 1,389 (the chart and the table count the unrated too). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bars<-by_rating bars$rating<-factor(bars$rating,levels=rev(levels(bars$rating))) colors<-rating_colors[as.character(bars$rating)] left<-plot_ly(bars,x=~share,y=~rating,type="bar",orientation="h",marker=list(color=colors), text=~percent(share,1),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the tornadoes (%{customdata:,})", customdata=~n,showlegend=FALSE) right<-plot_ly(bars,x=~death_share,y=~rating,type="bar",orientation="h",marker=list(color=colors), text=~percent(death_share,1),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the deaths (%{customdata:,})", customdata=~deaths,showlegend=FALSE) hidden_axis<-list(title="",showticklabels=FALSE,showgrid=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE) panel_title<-function(text,axis) { result<-list(text=text,xref=paste(axis,"domain"),yref="paper",x=0,y=1,xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=13)) return(result) } subplot(left,right,shareY=TRUE,margin=0.04,widths=c(0.5,0.5)) %>% chart(paste0("Tornadoes and deaths by rating, ",first_year,"–",last_year), paste0("NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Share of all tornadoes and of ", "all deaths; the table has the numbers."), x_axis=c(hidden_axis,list(range=c(0,1.7*max(bars$share)))), xaxis2=c(hidden_axis,list(range=c(0,1.7*max(bars$death_share)))), annotations=list(panel_title("Tornadoes","x"),panel_title("Deaths","x2")), margin=list(l=70,t=90,b=50,r=10),note_y=-0.06) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Which were the worst? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} deadliest<-head(tor[order(-tor$fat,-tor$inj),],8) # each year: the tornadoes, the deaths, the tornadoes of each rating and above, and the unrated by_year<-aggregate(cbind(n=1,deaths=fat,ef1=mag>=1,ef2=mag>=2,ef3=mag>=3,unrated=mag<0)~yr,data=tor, FUN=sum) worst_years<-by_year[order(-by_year$deaths),] # each day: the tornadoes, those of EF3 and above and the deaths, from the day with the most by_day<-aggregate(cbind(n=1,ef3=mag>=3,deaths=fat)~date,data=tor,FUN=sum) by_day<-by_day[order(-by_day$n),] top_days<-head(by_day,5) day_of<-function(d) { result<-by_day[by_day$date==d,] return(result) } record_day<-by_day[1,] n_100<-sum(tor$fat>=100) fat_50<-tor[tor$fat>=50,] ``` ::: **The deadliest tornado in the data killed 158 people, in Missouri on 22 May 2011.** The table has the eight deadliest. The data say how many died, not how many tornadoes struck places where people live: that is a question of where tornadoes land, and of warnings and shelter, which this page does not follow. --- ## 5. Are there more of them than there used to be? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} count_after<-function(x,years) { result<-mean(x[by_year$yr%in%years]) return(result) } trend_row<-function(name,x) { result<-data.frame(name=name, start=count_after(x,first_ten), end=count_after(x,last_ten), chance=chance(x,by_year$yr), stringsAsFactors=FALSE) return(result) } # the days of the year with at least one tornado of rating EF1 or above, and the days with ten or # more per_day<-aggregate(cbind(n=mag)~yr+date,data=tor[tor$mag>=1,],FUN=length) ef1_days<-aggregate(cbind(days=1,big_days=n>=10)~yr,data=per_day,FUN=sum) ef1_days<-merge(data.frame(yr=by_year$yr),ef1_days,all.x=TRUE) ef1_days[is.na(ef1_days)]<-0 changes<-rbind(trend_row("All tornadoes",by_year$n),trend_row("EF1 or above",by_year$ef1), trend_row("EF2 or above",by_year$ef2),trend_row("EF3 or above",by_year$ef3), trend_row("People killed",by_year$deaths), trend_row("Days with an EF1 or above",ef1_days$days), trend_row("Days with ten or more EF1 or above",ef1_days$big_days)) changes$change<-100*(changes$end/changes$start-1) of_change<-function(name,column) { result<-changes[[column]][changes$name==name] return(result) } # what if every unrated tornado were EF1 or above? chance_if_strong<-chance(by_year$ef1+by_year$unrated,by_year$yr) before_2007<-by_year$yr<2007 chance_before<-chance(by_year$ef1[before_2007],by_year$yr[before_2007]) chance_after<-chance(by_year$ef1[!before_2007],by_year$yr[!before_2007]) ef2_peak<-by_year$yr[which.max(by_year$ef2)] ef0<-by_year$n-by_year$ef1-by_year$unrated ef0_start<-count_after(ef0,first_ten) ef0_end<-count_after(ef0,last_ten) ``` ::: **More are reported, but the rise is mostly in the weak tornadoes.** In 1950–1959 the SPC database had 479 tornadoes a year, in 2016–2025 1,318: 175% more, and a rank test of all the years finds the rise (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is less than 1 in 100). Much of the rise is in the weakest tornadoes: EF0 tornadoes went from 105 a year to 534. A study of the database found that the doubling of the count from the 1950s to the 2000s "is likely not related to meteorological causes alone", and that the count of F1 and stronger tornadoes was steadier than that of F2 and stronger ([Verbout et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1175/waf910.1)); another says that changes in how tornadoes are reported "have made it difficult" to read the trend, and leaves out the weakest ([Brooks et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1257460)). Counting from EF1 up, the rise is smaller: 374 a year at the start and 632 at the end (+69%), and the test does not clearly find a trend (6 in 100). The table compares the first and the last ten years. The last column is the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as that of all the years without a trend. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(name=changes$name, start=number(changes$start), end=number(changes$end), change=change_text(changes$change), chance=changes$chance), col.names=c("",paste0(min(first_ten),"–",max(first_ten)), paste0(min(last_ten),"–",max(last_ten)),"Change","By chance, in 100"), align="lrrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | 1950–1959| 2016–2025| Change| By chance, in 100| |:----------------------------------|---------:|---------:|------:|-----------------:| |All tornadoes | 479| 1,318| +175%| less than 1| |EF1 or above | 374| 632| +69%| 6| |EF2 or above | 189| 142| −25%| less than 1| |EF3 or above | 50| 28| −43%| less than 1| |People killed | 142| 51| −64%| 4| |Days with an EF1 or above | 120| 110| −9%| less than 1| |Days with ten or more EF1 or above | 7| 18| +167%| less than 1| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panels<-c("All tornadoes","EF1 or above","EF2 or above","EF3 or above") series<-list(by_year$n,by_year$ef1,by_year$ef2,by_year$ef3) ten_year<-changes[match(panels,changes$name),] # one panel: the tornadoes of each year, and the averages of the first (blue) and the last ten years # (red) trend_panel<-function(k) { result<-plot_ly(x=by_year$yr,y=series[[k]],type="scatter",mode="lines+markers", line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1),marker=list(color=dark_gray,size=4), hovertemplate=paste0(panels[k],", %{x}: %{y:,}")) %>% add_segments(x=min(first_ten)-0.4,xend=max(first_ten)+0.4,y=ten_year$start[k], yend=ten_year$start[k],line=list(color=blue,width=3), hovertemplate=paste0("Average of ",min(first_ten),"–",max(first_ten), ": %{y:,.0f}"),inherit=FALSE) %>% add_segments(x=min(last_ten)-0.4,xend=max(last_ten)+0.4,y=ten_year$end[k],yend=ten_year$end[k], line=list(color=red,width=3), hovertemplate=paste0("Average of ",min(last_ten),"–",max(last_ten), ": %{y:,.0f}"),inherit=FALSE) %>% layout(xaxis=list(tick0=1950,dtick=20),yaxis=list(rangemode="tozero",tickformat=",")) return(result) } p<-subplot(lapply(1:4,trend_panel),nrows=2,shareX=TRUE,margin=c(0.03,0.03,0.08,0.08)) # the title of each panel, above it domains<-plotly_build(p)$x$layout panel_titles<-lapply(1:4,function(k) { x_axis<-c("xaxis","xaxis2")[(k-1)%%2+1] y_axis<-c("yaxis","yaxis2","yaxis3","yaxis4")[k] list(text=paste0("",panels[k],""),x=domains[[x_axis]]$domain[1],xref="paper", y=domains[[y_axis]]$domain[2],yref="paper",xanchor="left",yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE) }) p %>% chart("More tornadoes, or only more found?", paste0("NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Blue: the average of ",min(first_ten),"–", max(first_ten),"; red: of ",min(last_ten),"–",max(last_ten), ". Unrated tornadoes are in the first panel only."), annotations=panel_titles,showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=90,b=70),note_y=-0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **The strongest tornadoes are fewer, but be careful with that.** The EF2 and stronger tornadoes fell from 189 a year to 142 (by chance less than 1 in 100), the EF3 and stronger from 50 to 28 (less than 1 in 100). Their peak year was 1973. But ratings are judgements of damage, they changed from one scale to the other in 2007, and from 2007 the unrated tornadoes grew in number, so this page does not conclude that the strong tornadoes have become rarer. The unrated tornadoes matter for the count of EF1 and above: if every one of them is counted in it, the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend becomes 1 in 100, against 6. For the years before 2007 alone it is 95 in 100, and for 2007 on 3 in 100. People killed fell from 142 a year to 51 (4 in 100); these data do not say why. **What changed more is how the tornadoes come.** The days with at least one tornado of EF1 or above fell from 120.4 a year to 110.0, while the days with ten or more of them rose from 6.7 to 17.9 (the chances of the two patterns, less than 1 and less than 1 in 100). That is what a study of the database found, after setting aside the weakest tornadoes: the mean annual number "has remained relatively constant", but the variability has increased since the 1970s, with fewer days with tornadoes and more days with many ([Brooks et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1257460)). --- ## So, what does it mean? 1. **A few states have the most tornadoes for their size, and they are not the largest.** Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois had the most per area from 2006 to 2025, and Texas, the state with the most tornadoes, only 24th. Canada's project finds about 112 a year, against 1,346 in the United States, but the two are not counted the same way. 2. **They come in the afternoon and evening, mostly in spring.** 22% of them began in May, and each part of the country has its own busiest month. 3. **Most are weak and most deaths come from the strongest.** EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of the tornadoes and 61% of the deaths. 4. **The worst years and days are far from the average.** 27 April 2011 had 210 tornadoes in one day, and 2011 killed 553 people. 5. **More are counted, but that is not the same as more.** The tornadoes of EF2 and above did not rise; what has changed is that the tornadoes of EF1 and above come on fewer days and in bigger groups. **What this does not show.** There is no worldwide count: the data cover the United States and, in outline, Canada, and say nothing of the many countries where tornadoes are not systematically recorded, so this page cannot say that the United States has the most tornadoes in the world, only the most that are counted. Reports depend on who is there to see a tornado, and the ratings on what it destroyed. Averages by state hide the differences inside a state, and a rank test says whether a pattern is likely to be chance, not what causes it. And the counts say nothing of the people who live where tornadoes land.
